analysis.one_liner: Rewrites labor law so most lead workers and skilled tradespeople count as employees who can unionize, not supervisors who cannot.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House committee 26-20 in September 2007 with 164 cosponsors, but never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal labor law, employees labeled 'supervisors' cannot join unions. This bill narrows that label: only someone who spends the majority of their work time actually exercising authority over other workers counts as a supervisor, and it removes 'assigning' work and 'directing' crews as automatic disqualifiers. That would let many skilled tradespeople, lead workers, and professionals — groups the bill's name highlights — join or stay in unions. The bill cleared its House committee but never came to the floor for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Skilled and professional workers, construction tradesworkers, and lead employees currently classified as supervisors because they assign or direct other workers, even when that is not most of their job. If they count as employees under the National Labor Relations Act, they regain the legal right to organize, bargain collectively, and be protected from retaliation for union activity.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that a person exercise supervisory authority for a majority of their work time to be counted as a supervisor, so occasional or incidental direction of co-workers no longer strips a worker of union rights.

Removes the power to assign work and the responsibility to direct crews from the legal definition of supervisor, which was the basis for excluding many charge nurses, foremen, and lead workers from union membership.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — particularly construction firms, hospitals, and manufacturers — lose the ability to keep lead workers out of unions by labeling them supervisors, and would face more organizing drives and collective bargaining obligations among their skilled and frontline workforce.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing new organizing among lead workers

drawbacks.text: The bill changes a balance struck in the National Labor Relations Act: employers argue that workers who assign or direct others, even part-time, need to be treated as part of management so the employer retains a reliable chain of command, and that narrowing the definition opens the door to lawsuits and disputes over worktime calculations in nearly every organizing case.

Employees newly reclassified from supervisor to rank-and-file status would become subject to union rules they previously sat outside, including dues requirements and union-imposed work rules, and some who value a management-track role could lose it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a concrete restoration of union rights for a specific group — skilled workers and lead employees who supervise others incidentally but work mostly with their hands or their tools — and the cost falls on employers who benefit from excluding those workers from unions. The main design risk is a new fact-finding burden over how much of each worker's time counts as supervisory, which would be litigated case by case; that is a real cost but not one that changes who gains and who loses.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee voted 26-20 in September 2007 to send the bill to the floor, but it was never scheduled for a vote there, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2007 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
On September 19, 2007, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported (amended) by a vote of 26-20 — a narrow margin that fell along party lines in a Democratic-majority committee.
No further action followed: the bill was never reported to the floor for a vote in 2007 or 2008, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with the bill unfinished.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who keep lead workers and skilled tradespeople out of unions by classifying them as supervisors, since the legal definition they rely on was never changed. Nurses, construction foremen, and other lead workers who would have gained organizing rights got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew 164 cosponsors including 5 Republicans, but the committee's 26-20 vote to send it out was essentially a Democratic-majority roll call with Republicans opposed.

industries.industry: Employers (construction, hospitals, manufacturers, and other firms with lead workers)
industries.note: If the bill had passed, employers could no longer exclude union-eligible employees simply by labeling them supervisors for assigning or directing work. They would face more organizing among skilled and frontline staff and would have to bargain with newly organized units — a cost that is the workers' corresponding gain.

The bill would open union membership to tens of thousands of workers currently barred as supervisors, expanding the potential membership and bargaining units for unions organizing in construction, health care, and manufacturing.
